SAMUEL GOODALE.
The Rev. Samuel Goodale, D. D., one of the seven
founders of the Fraternity, was born December 20, 18 14, in
South Egremont, Massachusetts, in a beautiful vale among
the mountains of Southern Berkshire�
a
region well calculated
to develop both physical and mental energy. His father was
a revolutionary soldier, and by profession a school teacher.
His early education was such as could be gained in the com
mon schools of that day; but about 1827 an
academy was
established in the village and better facilities were offered for
education, so that a systematic course of study preparatory
for college was pursued by Mr. Goodale, and finally he entered
Union College, Schenectady, New York, as a
Sophomore in
1833Though college expenses in those days were slight, yet
there were many financial problems to be solved, and school
teaching in winter seemed to be for Mr. Goodale the only
solution. His scholarship in all branches of study was-uniformly high. He was elected a member of Phi Beta Kappa,
and was honorably graduated in 1836.
Dr. Goodale says that his ambition throughout his college
course was to qualify himself to be a teacher or
college pro
fessor; and accordingly, after remaining at home for a few
weeks subsequently to his graduation, he was furnished with a
letter of introduction from Governor Briggs of Massachusetts
to Henry Clay of Kentucky, and he entered into a
partial
engagement for a school at Lexington. Passing through New
York, Philadelphia, and Pittsburg, a passage was secured by
steamboat to Louisville. Circumstances he could not control
occasioned a
delay at Wheeling, and thus the whole course of
his life was altered. Through the influence of a friend he
secured a
professorship in the Wheeling Institute, at that day
and for
many years after a
prominent academy.

128 THE PSI UPSILON REVIEW.
His years at Wheeling passed by most satisfactorily, but
his plans through some mysterious agency were changed, and
he resolved to become a student of theology. Accordingly he
removed from Wheeling in the summer of 1838, and entered
the General Theological Seminary of the Episcopal Church in
New York City, where he remained until 1841. Then he was
ordained in Providence, R. I.
Spending a few years in rather unsatisfactory ministerial
work in central New York, he finally received a call in 1850
to the Episcopal Church at Kalamazoo, Mich. ; but his restless
spirit seemed to prompt him to more active labors, and he
became a pioneer missionary, usually, going in advance of all
railroads. Going to Nebraska in 1866, he has since been
engaged continually in missionary endeavor, building churches
and organizing congregations in many important cities. When
he had reached the age of seventy-five years, his active parish
work seemed to be ended, and he quietly returned to his home
in Columbus, where it is expected he will remain the rest of
his life.
As a
clergyman he is probably as well known as any of
the clergy of Nebraska, having been one of the Honorary
Canons of Trinity Cathedral, Omaha,.since it was first organ
ized, and having been several times elected deputy to the
General Convention of the Protestant Episcopal Church. He
received the degree of Doctor of Divinity from Nebraska
College in 1883.
As one of the five survivors of the little group by which,
more than sixty-two years ago, Psi Upsilon was founded, he
is greatly revered by the Fraternity, and has received many
marks of consideration from the chapters and members.
During recent years he has visited several of the branches and
city clubs of the Society, and it is hoped that he will attend
the convention at Ann Arbor next May.
Notwithstanding his great age
�
for he is now more than
eighty-one years old�Dr. Goodale is erect and vigorous; his
eyes are clear, and his voice is firm. To more than eight
thousand younger members he furnishes an illustrious example
of plain Hving and
high thinking.

THE FINCH DINNER.
Francis Miles Finch, the poet laureate of Psi Upsilon,
was initiated into the Beta (Yale) Chapter of the Fraternity
in July, 1 847. During his Junior year he wrote the celebrated
"Psi Upsilon Smoking Song", "The Mystical Bower", "The
Halls of Psi Upsilon", "The Fairies' Song", and the
"Anthem", all of which are to be found in the first edition
(1849) of our Song-Book. In later years he has composed
other songs and poems for the Society. As Professor Willard
Fiske truly says "no Psi Upsilon song-writer has filled so
large a
place, for nearly half a century, in the social life of
the Fraternity, as 'Psi U. Finch'". .
Outside of the Psi Upsilon, Judge Finch is more widely
known by his "Nathan Hale" and "The Blue and the Gray"
�
lyrical compositions perfect in every requirement demanded
in the field of patriotic minstrelsy; and his "Storm, the
King", originally made public, like "The Blue and the Gray"
in the pages of The Atlantic Monthly, is one of the most
striking of the productions belonging to the school of Poe.
The political effect of "The Blue and the Gray" in both sec
tions of the Union�
then so
recently opposed to each other
on the field of battle�
it is not easy to overestimate.
The broad, intellectual culture, the discriminating taste,
the literary facility, and the pure, terse English displayed in
Judge Finch's verse, are also manifest in the judicial opinions
delivered by him during his fourteen years' service in the Court
of Appeals of New York ; nor does the remarkable style of
those decisions detract from the legal ability and equitable
judgment which they evince.
"His literary career", says Dr. Fiske, "considering the
high quality of his work, has run on a
singularly unobtrusive
way
�
devoid of any of that reclame which is too often deemed
essential, in this advertising age, even in the domain of letters.
His life as a laborious advocate in what was
long only a
pleasing country village, was succeeded by a decade and a
half of almost equally absorbing activity in connection with
the State's highest tribuna,l. Only once�
except iri the com-

did he ever devote his
energies to" any task beyond the limits of his profession and
office. In political struggles he never
engaged. But he gave
much of his time and thought to the inception and organiza
tion of Cornell University. Next to the self-sacrificing devo
tion of another Yale Psi Upsilon, Andrew Dickson White
(Beta '53), that institution, which in a
single generation was
founded, greyv up and took its place among the foremost of
American universities, owes its greatest debt to the keen and
farseeing judgment and the watchful zeal in the earliest year,
of Francis Miles Finch, now the honored head of the faculty
of law ".
On the evening of Friday, January 24, 1896, a dinner
was given at the Hotel Savoy, New York City, under the
auspices of the Psi Upsilon Club, in honor of the distinguished
poet and jurist to whom the Fraternity is so deeply indebted.
The key-note to the celebration was struck in these words
from one of Judge Finch's own songs :
"Then till the sands of life are run,
We'll sing to thee, Psi Upsilon" !
"What's the matter with Finch".? "He's all right" in
chorus, at frequent intervals, gave substantial evidence of the
esteem in which the guest of the evening was held. One
hundred and fifty brothers, representing all but one of the col
leges and chapters of the Fraternity, were present at the
reception and banquet. The classes represented ranged from
'39 to '99.
After a
reception in the parlors, the company adjourned
to the dining-room, to the strains of a
string quartet. As
soon as

dainty but substantial menu. At the guest table the Hon.
Theodore Bacon, Yale, '53, presided. On his right were
Judge Finch, Prof. H. S. Williams of Yale, Judges Addison
Brown, Charles F. MacLean, and Nathaniel H. Clement,
Thomas Thacher, and the Rev. Dr. George R. Van De
Water; on his left. Dr. George Henry Fox, president of the

THE FINCH DINNER. 137
Forsaking then the Olympian way,
Our Finch a
jealous mistress wooed,
And found her kind �
so kind, men say,
Who sneer at the poetic mood�
"In faith she must be blind"!
She took the rhymster in her arms,
And placed him in her highest seat,
And bade him only sing her charms,
In unrhymed measures, as is meet,.
Within her tuneless courts.
Long time to her he constant proved.
And strayed not from the toilsome way,
But made the jade believe he loved.
No other sort of work or play,
But writing her "Reports".
Now Scholar, Jurist, Poet, Sage,
He shuts at last the leathern lid
Of that strange tome, on every page
Of which, 'mid many words, is hid
Some formal guess at truth.
God grant that armed with fluent pen,
With tender heart and teeming brain,
In poesie's sweet field again,
He wander long and sing again.
The melodies of Youth.

Psi Upsilon salutes her son,

In welcoming Judge Finch to his new duties as Dean of
the Cornell Law School, Bro. Austin Abbott well expressed
the sentiment of his hearers as follows :
"We congratulate the Law School whose students are to
enjoy the instructions of one who speaking with the voice of

138 THE PSI. UPSILON REVIEW.
authority for the court of last resort, has for so many years
instructed and charmed the bar ; and we congratulate the
cause of legal education on the accession of one whose bril
liant gifts, sound learning and long experience in affairs will
make him welcome in its foremost ranks, and whose spirit
and example will aid all who are seeking to teach the citizens
of a free republic how to appreciate and respect the law on
which its liberties depend ".
A special delegation of four undergraduates- came from
New Haven to attend the dinner, and the Boston Psi Upsilon
Club sent as a
delegate W. L. Sage. The festivities contin
ued until long after midnight.
The Brooklyn Standard-Union spoke editorially as fol
lows concerning the dinner :
' '
The tribute of the Psi Upsilon Fraternity last evening,
to its honored member, a
poet of national and permanent
fame, a jurist of honorable and untarnished record, was a
success, brilliant and unique, in a calendar crowded with
similar functions. Underneath the public and formal compli
ment, it was easy to perceive the substantial fraternal feeling,
of which the outward manifestation was the natural and spon
taneous expression, an evidence of a bond as lasting as life,
and as intimate as that which joins the members of the same
family. Judge Finch passes the consummation of his career
to a
repose, not idleness, honorably earned, gratefully appre
ciated by his brethren of all ages in the Fraternity, in which
they are not alone, but include with them the great body of'
their fellow citizens. The most confirmed skeptic, the most
ignorant and inveterate critic of Greek-letter Fraternities,
<
realizing the truth concerning last night's incident, and the
facts which evoked and justified it, would, if honest and intel
ligent, either terminate his 'innocuous desuetude' or expend
it in other directions. The list of the red-letter days of '
the
noble old Fraternity' grows steadily larger, and its vigor and
vitality increase with its years ".

THE DETROIT ALUMNI ASSOCIATION.
This Association was organized in 1877, 'when the total
number of Psi U. men
residing in Detroit was
twenty. A new
list containing the names of seventy-nine brothers, all resi
dents of the City of the Straits, has been compiled. Of these,
forty-seven are members of the Phi, the remaining thirty-two
being distributed among twelve other chapters, thus: Theta,
five; Delta, two; Beta, five; Gamma, one; Zeta, one; Lambda,
one; Xi, three; Alpha, two; Upsilon, one; Iota, three; Chi,
one; Beta Beta, seven.
Seventeen are undergraduates in college, fourteen at the
University of Michigan, two at Trinity, and one at Yale.
Among the older members are Elisha Taylor (Theta '37),
and Clement M. Davison (Theta '38), both well-known citi
zens of Detroit, and whose long connection of more than
sixty years with Psi Upsilon runs back to the earliest days of
the Fraternity; the Rt. Rev. Thomas Frederick Davies, S. T.
D. (Beta '53), Bishop of Michigan; the Hon. Alfred Russell,
LL. D. (Zeta '50), formerly United States' District Attorney,
and one of the most eminent lawyers of Michigan; the Rev.
Rufus W. Clark, D.D. (Delta '65), Rector of St. Paul's
Church; William G. Thompson (Gamma '62), ex-Mayor of
Detroit; and Albert M. Henry (Phi '67), a
prominent citizen,
and one of the charter members of the Phi.
Nine of the seventy-nine Psi U. men in Detroit are sons
of members of the Fraternity. Among these representatives
of the second generation are the sons of Bishops Davies and
Paddock, a son of the distinguished Presbyterian clergyman
Dr. William Aikman (Delta '46), of Atlantic City, New Jersey,
and a son of the well-known citizen, lawyer, and politician,
Orlando M. Barnes (Phi '50), of Lansing, Michigan. Were
one to enumerate the prospective contributions to Psi Upsilon
from among the youthful scions of enthusiastic Detroit mem
bers. The Review would need enlargement.
The' recent losses by death in the Detroit Association
have been painfully numerous. William Stagg (Phi '70),
Cashier of the Wayne County Savings' Bank; Norman C,

What relations should a branch of Psi Upsilon have with
branches of other college fraternities existing at the same
institution.? None whatever. Our Fraternity was instituted
for certain special purposes which relate to and concern its
members alone. Psi Upsilon was not formed to assist in
centrolling college politics, or in publishing annuals, or in
giving "germans", or in doing anything in concert with other
societies. We care not for recognition as a
part of a
general
fraternity system which we ourselves never have recognized,
and which we are
logically incapacitated from recognizing.
Gatherings of alumni such as have occurred during the
present college year in New York, Washington, Rochester,
Grand Rapids, Boston, and other cities, prove how strong is
the Psi Upsilon tie, and also illustrate, by the attendance of
many distinguished men, the large representation of our
Society in the upper walks of life. It is to be regretted that
want of room forbids our giving full accounts of the reunion
held at Grand Rapids on the evening of December 23, and of
the dinner at Rochester November 19.

consent of the nineteen active chapters has been given to
the organization of a new branch of Psi Upsilon in the

taken; though it must not be forgotten that forty years ago a

their old relations before any aid or encouragement in the
direction of Psi Upsilon could be given to them. They
resigned their membership and instituted a local order, which
they named Rho Kappa Upsilon. The first letter of this

Henry D. A. Ward (Beta '42), a lineal descendant of
Gen. Artemas Ward, died in Middletown, Conn., Dec. 17,
1895, at the age of 74. He was a
graduate of Yale in the
class of 1842, and of the Harvard Law School. He formerly
lived in Detroit, Mich. ,
but returned to Connecticut in 1 864,
and since then has been engaged in literary work. Mr. Ward
was first lieutenant of the Mansfield Guard, and of late was
weather observer of the United States government. He
leaves no family.
Andrew D. White (Beta '53), one of the Venezuela Com
mission, was born at Homer, N. Y. ,
Nov. 7, 1832. He went
to Yale after spending one
year at Hobart College. From
1853 to 1856 he travelled in Europe, after which he for a
short time studied law in New Haven. From 1857 to 1862
he was Professor of History and English Literature in the
University of Michigan. In 1865 he was elected President of
Cornell University, where he was also Professor of History.
He was Senator from the State of New York in 1864-65, and
again in 1866-67; United States Commissioner to the Centen
nial Exposition in 1876; Commissioner to the Paris Exposi
tion in 1878, being the American Representative on the jury
of appeals; and United States Minister Plenopotentiary to
Germany 1879-81. He has been, at times, President of
the Syracuse National bank, and a director in the New York
Central Railroad compariies. He resigned from the Presidency
of Cornell permanently in 1892, on his being appointed Min
ister to Russia by President Harrison. He resigned his
ministry after a short service, and has since devoted himself
to literary work and to lecturing. His son, Frederick Davies
White (named after the Rt. Rev. Thomas Frederick Davies,
Beta '53), entered Cornell University and our Chi Chapter
in 1876.
